title: Verification of Truth Tables of Logic Gates Using Multisim

questions.q: Why are NAND and NOR gates called universal gates?
questions.a: Because any Boolean function (NOT, AND, OR, XOR, etc.) can be implemented using only NAND gates or only NOR gates.

questions.q: Why is an XOR gate also called an inequality detector or odd-parity gate?
questions.a: Because its output is 1 if and only if its two inputs are unequal (01 or 10), which corresponds to an odd number of 1s.

questions.q: How do you make a NOT gate from a 2-input NAND or NOR gate?
questions.a: Tie both input terminals of the NAND (or NOR) gate together to the same input signal A, or tie one input of a NAND gate to logic 1.

questions.q: How many rows are in the truth table of an N-input logic gate?
questions.a: 2^N rows (4 rows for 2 inputs, 8 rows for 3 inputs).

questions.q: How areXOR and XNOR expressed in Python bitwise/boolean logic?
questions.a: XOR is `A ^ B`, and XNOR is `int(not (A ^ B))` or `int(A == B)`.

questions.q: What happens if a TTL 74xx gate input is left unconnected (floating)?
questions.a: A floating TTL input typically acts as a logic HIGH (1), which can cause unexpected truth table readings and noise pickup.

questions.q: If A = 1 and B = 0, what are the outputs of NAND, NOR, XOR, and XNOR?
Why must truth tables be generated by a deterministic Boolean engine rather than guessed by an LLM?
questions.a: Deterministic evaluation guarantees 100% accuracy for every minterm row without arithmetic or token hallucination.

questions.q: For which input combinations do OR and XOR produce different outputs?
questions.a: Only for (A=1, B=1), where OR outputs 1 and XOR outputs 0.
